He was afraid they were robbers, and climbed into a tree for safety.

They unbridled their horses and tied them to trees.

At last the door opened again, and the Forty Thieves came out.
As the Captain went in last he came out first, and made them all pass

he then closed the door, saying: "Shut, Sesame!"
Every man bridled his horse and mounted, the Captain put himself at their head, and

he could not sleep, and went to his brother in the morning before sunrise. "Ali

By this Ali Baba perceived that through his wife's folly Cassim and his wife knew

pages.caption: He soon found the place, and the door in the rock. He said: "Open, Sesame!"
pages.description: [figure speaking magic words at rock face]

pages.caption: and the door opened and shut behind him.
He could have feasted his eyes all day on the treasures, but he now hastened
to gather together as much of it as possible; but when he was ready to
go he could not remember what to say for thinking of his great riches. Instead
of "Sesame," he said: "Open, Barley!" and the door remained fast.
He named several different sorts of grain, all but the right one, and the door
still stuck fast. He was so frightened at the danger he was in that he
had as much forgotten the word as if he had never heard it.
About noon the robbers returned to their cave, and saw Cassim's mules roving about with
great chests on their backs. This gave them the alarm; they drew their sabres, and
went to the door, which opened on their Captain's saying: "Open, Sesame!"
Cassim, who had heard the trampling of their horses' feet, resolved to sell his life
dearly,
so when the door opened he leaped out and threw the Captain down.
In vain, however, for the robbers with their sabres soon killed him.
On entering the cave they saw all the bags laid ready, and could not imagine
how anyone had got in without knowing their secret.
They cut Cassim's body into four quarters, and nailed them up inside the cave, in
order to frighten anyone who should venture in, and went away in search of more
treasure.
As night drew on Cassim's wife grew very uneasy, and ran to her brother-in-law, and
pages.scene: Cassim's wife running to Ali Baba

pages.caption: told him where her husband had gone.
pages.scene: Cassim's wife running to Ali Baba

pages.caption: Ali Baba did his best to comfort her, and set out to the forest in
search of Cassim.
The first thing he saw on entering the cave was his dead brother.
Full of horror, he put the body on one of his asses, and bags of
pages.scene: Ali Baba carrying body on ass

pages.caption: gold on the other two, and, covering all with some fagots, returned home.
pages.scene: Ali Baba carrying body on ass

pages.caption: He drove the two asses laden with gold into his own yard, and led the
other to Cassim's house. The door was opened by the slave Morgiana, whom he knew
to be both brave and cunning. Unloading the ass, he said to her: "This is
the body of your master, who has been murdered, but whom we must bury as
though he had died in his bed."
I will speak with you again, but now tell your mistress I am come." The
wife of Cassim, on learning the fate of her husband, broke out into cries and
tears,
but Ali Baba offered to take her to live with him and his wife if
she would promise to keep his counsel and leave everything to Morgiana; whereupon she agreed,
and dried her eyes.
Morgiana, meanwhile, sought an apothecary and asked him for some lozenges. "My poor master," she
said,
"can neither eat nor speak, and no one knows what his distemper is."
She carried home the lozenges and returned next day weeping, and asked for an essence
only given to those just about to die. Thus, in the evening, no one was
surprised to hear the wretched shrieks and cries of Cassim's wife and Morgiana, telling everyone
that Cassim was dead.
The day after Morgiana went to an old cobbler near the gates of the town
who opened his stall early, put a piece of gold in his hand, and bade
him follow her with his needle and thread. Having bound his eyes with a handkerchief,
she took him to the room where the body lay, pulled off the bandage, and
bade him sew the quarters together, after which she covered his eyes again and led
him home.
Then they buried Cassim, and Morgiana his slave followed him to the grave, weeping and
tearing her hair, while Cassim's wife stayed at home uttering lamentable cries. Next day she
went to live with Ali Baba, who gave Cassim's shop to his eldest son.
The Forty Thieves, on their return to the cave, were much astonished to find Cassim's
body gone and some of their money-bags. "We are certainly discovered," said the Captain, "and
shall be undone if we cannot find out who it is that knows our secret."
To this end one of you who is bold and artful must go into the
pages.scene: Thief disguised as traveler entering town

pages.caption: city dressed as a traveler, and discover whom we have killed, and whether men talk
pages.scene: Thief disguised as traveler entering town

pages.caption: of the strange manner of his death." One of the thieves started up and offered
pages.scene: Thief disguised as traveler entering town

pages.caption: to do this, and after the rest had highly commended him for his bravery he
pages.scene: Thief disguised as traveler entering town

pages.caption: disguised himself,
pages.scene: Thief disguised as traveler entering town

pages.caption: and happened to enter the town at daybreak, just by Baba Mustapha's stall.
pages.scene: Thief disguised as traveler entering town

pages.caption: The thief bade him good-day, saying: "Honest man, how can you possibly see to stitch
at your age?" "Old as I am," replied the cobbler, "I have very good eyes,
and will you believe me when I tell you that I sewed a dead body
together in a place where I had less light than I have now."
The robber was overjoyed at his good fortune, and, giving him a piece of gold,
desired to be shown the house where he stitched up the dead body.
At first Mustapha refused, saying that he had been blindfolded; but when the robber gave
him another piece of gold he began to think he might remember the turnings if
blindfolded as before. This means succeeded; the robber partly led him, and was partly guided
by him,
right in front of Cassim's house, the door of which the robber marked with a
piece of chalk.
Then, well pleased, he bade farewell to Baba Mustapha and returned to the forest.
By and by Morgiana, going out, saw the mark the robber had made, quickly guessed
that some mischief was brewing, and fetching a piece of chalk marked two or three
doors on each side, without saying anything to her master or mistress.
The thief, meantime, told his comrades of his discovery. The Captain thanked him, and bade
pages.scene: Thieves confused by multiple chalk marks

pages.caption: him show him the house he had marked. But when they came to it they
pages.scene: Thieves confused by multiple chalk marks

pages.caption: saw that five or six of the houses were chalked in the same manner.
pages.scene: Thieves confused by multiple chalk marks

pages.caption: The guide was so confounded that he knew not what answer to make, and when
they returned he was at once beheaded for having failed.
Another robber was dispatched, and, having won over Baba Mustapha, marked the house in red
pages.scene: Second thief marking house in red

pages.caption: chalk;

pages.caption: The Captain now resolved to go himself, but, wiser than the others, he did not
mark the house, but looked at it so closely that he could not fail to
remember it.
He returned, and ordered his men to go into the neighboring villages and buy nineteen
mules,
and thirty-eight leather jars, all empty except one, which was full of oil.
The Captain put one of his men, fully armed, into each, rubbing the outside of
the jars with oil from the full vessel. Then the nineteen mules were loaded with
thirty-seven robbers in jars, and the jar of oil, and reached the town by dusk.
The Captain stopped his mules in front of Ali Baba's house, and said to Ali

pages.caption: Baba,
pages.scene: Captain arriving at Ali Baba's house

pages.caption: who was sitting outside for coolness: "I have brought some oil from a distance to
pages.scene: Captain arriving at Ali Baba's house

pages.caption: sell at to-morrow's market, but it is now so late that I know not where
pages.scene: Captain arriving at Ali Baba's house

pages.caption: to pass the night, unless you will do me the favor to take me in."
pages.scene: Captain arriving at Ali Baba's house

pages.caption: Though Ali Baba had seen the Captain of the robbers in the forest, he did
not recognize him in the disguise of an oil merchant. He bade him welcome, opened
his gates for the mules to enter, and went to Morgiana to bid her prepare
a bed and supper for his guest.
He brought the stranger into his hall, and after they had supped went again to
pages.scene: Captain signaling to men in jars

pages.caption: speak to Morgiana in the kitchen, while the Captain went into the yard under pretense
pages.scene: Captain signaling to men in jars

pages.caption: of seeing after his mules, but really to tell his men what to do.
pages.scene: Captain signaling to men in jars

pages.caption: Beginning at the first jar and ending at the last, he said to each man:
pages.scene: Captain giving instructions to hidden men

pages.caption: She then told Abdallah, her fellow-slave, to set on the pot to make some broth
for her master, who had gone to bed. Meanwhile her lamp went out, and she
had no more oil in the house. "Do not be uneasy," said Abdallah; "go into
the yard and take some out of one of those jars." Morgiana thanked him for
his advice,
took the oil pot, and went into the yard. When she came to the first
jar the robber inside said softly: "Is it time?"
Any other slave but Morgiana, on finding a man in the jar instead of the
oil she wanted, would have screamed and made a noise; but she, knowing the danger
her master was in, bethought herself of a plan, and answered quietly: "Not yet, but
presently." She went to all the jars, giving the same answer, till she came to
the jar of oil.
She now saw that her master, thinking to entertain an oil merchant, had let thirty-eight
pages.scene: Morgiana pouring boiling oil into jars

pages.caption: robbers into his house. She filled her oil pot, went back to the kitchen, and,
pages.scene: Morgiana pouring boiling oil into jars

pages.caption: having lit her lamp, went again to the oil jar and filled a large kettle
pages.scene: Morgiana pouring boiling oil into jars

pages.caption: full of oil. When it boiled she went and poured enough oil into every jar
pages.scene: Morgiana pouring boiling oil into jars

pages.caption: to stifle and kill the robber inside.
pages.scene: Morgiana pouring boiling oil into jars

pages.caption: When this brave deed was done she went back to the kitchen, put out the
fire and the lamp, and waited to see what would happen.
In a quarter of an hour the Captain of the robbers awoke, got up, and
pages.scene: Captain discovering dead robbers in jars

pages.caption: opened the window. As all seemed quiet, he threw down some little pebbles which hit
pages.scene: Captain discovering dead robbers in jars

pages.caption: the jars.
pages.scene: Captain discovering dead robbers in jars

pages.caption: He listened, and as none of his men seemed to stir he grew uneasy, and
pages.scene: Captain discovering dead robbers in jars

pages.caption: went down into the yard. On going to the first jar and saying, "Are you
pages.scene: Captain discovering dead robbers in jars

pages.caption: asleep?" he smelt the hot boiled oil, and knew at once that his plot to
pages.scene: Captain discovering dead robbers in jars

pages.caption: murder Ali Baba and his household had been discovered.
pages.scene: Captain discovering dead robbers in jars

pages.caption: He found all the gang was dead, and, missing the oil out of the last
jar,
became aware of the manner of their death. He then forced the lock of a
door leading into a garden, and climbing over several walls made his escape.
Morgiana heard and saw all this, and, rejoicing at her success, went to bed and
fell asleep.
At daybreak Ali Baba arose, and, seeing the oil jars still there, asked why the
pages.scene: Ali Baba discovering man in jar

pages.caption: merchant had not gone with his mules. Morgiana bade him look in the first jar
pages.scene: Ali Baba discovering man in jar

pages.caption: and see if there was any oil. Seeing a man, he started back in terror.
pages.scene: Ali Baba discovering man in jar

pages.caption: "Have no fear," said Morgiana; "the man cannot harm you: he is dead." Ali Baba,
when he had recovered somewhat from his astonishment, asked what had become of the merchant.
"Merchant!" said she, "he is no more a merchant than I am!" and she told
him the whole story, assuring him that it was a plot of the robbers of
the forest,
of whom only three were left, and that the white and red chalk marks had
something to do with it.
Ali Baba at once gave Morgiana her freedom, saying that he owed her his life.
They then buried the bodies in Ali Baba's garden, while the mules were sold in
the market by his slaves.
The Captain returned to his lonely cave, which seemed frightful to him without his lost
pages.scene: Captain disguised as merchant in town

pages.caption: companions,
pages.scene: Captain disguised as merchant in town

pages.caption: and firmly resolved to avenge them by killing Ali Baba. He dressed himself carefully, and
pages.scene: Captain disguised as merchant in town

pages.caption: went into the town, where he took lodgings in an inn.
pages.scene: Captain disguised as merchant in town

pages.caption: In the course of a great many journeys to the forest he carried away many
pages.scene: Captain setting up shop opposite Ali Baba's son

pages.caption: rich stuffs and much fine linen, and set up a shop opposite that of Ali
pages.scene: Captain setting up shop opposite Ali Baba's son

pages.caption: Baba's son.
pages.scene: Captain setting up shop opposite Ali Baba's son

pages.caption: He called himself Cogia Hassan, and as he was both civil and well dressed he
pages.scene: Captain setting up shop opposite Ali Baba's son

pages.caption: soon made friends with Ali Baba's son, and through him with Ali Baba, whom he
pages.scene: Captain setting up shop opposite Ali Baba's son

pages.caption: was continually asking to sup with him.
pages.scene: Captain setting up shop opposite Ali Baba's son

pages.caption: Ali Baba, wishing to return his kindness, invited him into his house and received him
pages.scene: Ali Baba inviting merchant to supper

pages.caption: smiling,
pages.scene: Ali Baba inviting merchant to supper

pages.caption: thanking him for his kindness to his son. When the merchant was about to take
pages.scene: Ali Baba inviting merchant to supper

pages.caption: his leave Ali Baba stopped him, saying: "Where are you going, sir, in such haste?
pages.scene: Ali Baba inviting merchant to supper

pages.caption: Will you not stay and sup with me?"
pages.scene: Ali Baba inviting merchant to supper

pages.caption: The merchant refused, saying that he had a reason; and, on Ali Baba's asking him
what that was, he replied: "It is, sir, that I can eat no victuals that
have any salt in them." "If that is all," said Ali Baba, "let me tell
you that there shall be no salt in either the meat or the bread that
we eat to-night."
He went to give this order to Morgiana, who was much surprised. "Who is this
man," she said, "who eats no salt with his meat?" "He is an honest man,
Morgiana," returned her master; "therefore do as I bid you." But she could not withstand
a desire to see this strange man, so she helped Abdallah to carry up the
dishes,
and saw in a moment that Cogia Hassan was the robber Captain, and carried a
dagger under his garment.
"I am not surprised," she said to herself, "that this wicked man, who intends to
kill my master, will eat no salt with him; but I will hinder his plans."
She sent up the supper by Abdallah, while she made ready for one of the
boldest acts that could be thought on. When the dessert had been served, Cogia Hassan
was left alone with Ali Baba and his son, whom he thought to make drunk
and then to murder them. Morgiana, meanwhile, put on a head-dress like a dancing-girl's, and
clasped a girdle round her waist, from which hung a dagger with a silver hilt,
and said to Abdallah: "Take your tabor, and let us go and divert our master
and his guest."
Abdallah took his tabor and played before Morgiana until they came to the door, where
Abdallah stopped playing and Morgiana made a low courtesy. "Come in, Morgiana," said Ali Baba,
"and let Cogia Hassan see what you can do"; and, turning to Cogia Hassan, he
said:
"She's my slave and my housekeeper."
Cogia Hassan was by no means pleased, for he feared that his chance of killing
Ali Baba was gone for the present; but he pretended great eagerness to see Morgiana,
and Abdallah began to play and Morgiana to dance.
After she had performed several dances she drew her dagger and made passes with it,
sometimes pointing it at her own breast, sometimes at her master's, as if it were
part of the dance.
Suddenly, out of breath, she snatched the tabor from Abdallah with her left hand, and,
pages.scene: Morgiana plunging dagger into captain's heart

pages.caption: holding the dagger in her right hand, held out the tabor to her master. Ali
pages.scene: Morgiana plunging dagger into captain's heart

pages.caption: Baba and his son put a piece of gold into it, and Cogia Hassan, seeing
pages.scene: Morgiana plunging dagger into captain's heart

pages.caption: that she was coming to him, pulled out his purse to make her a present,
pages.scene: Morgiana plunging dagger into captain's heart

pages.caption: but while he was putting his hand into it Morgiana plunged the dagger into his
pages.scene: Morgiana plunging dagger into captain's heart

pages.caption: heart.
pages.scene: Morgiana plunging dagger into captain's heart

pages.caption: "Unhappy girl!" cried Ali Baba and his son, "what have you done to ruin us?"
pages.scene: Ali Baba and son crying out in shock

pages.caption: "It was to preserve you, master, not to ruin you," answered Morgiana. "See here," opening
the false merchant's garment and showing the dagger; "see what an enemy you have entertained!
Remember,
he would eat no salt with you, and what more would you have? Look at
him! he is both the false oil merchant and the Captain of the Forty Thieves."
Ali Baba was so grateful to Morgiana for thus saving his life that he offered
pages.scene: Ali Baba offering Morgiana to his son

pages.caption: her to his son in marriage, who readily consented, and a few days after the
pages.scene: Ali Baba offering Morgiana to his son

pages.caption: wedding was celebrated with greatest splendor.
